newsitem.title: USA: New NYMEX home has more room but bad acoustics.
newsitem.headline: New NYMEX home has more room but bad acoustics.

text.p: The New York Mercantile Exchange is celebrating its 125th anniversary by quadrupling the size of its trading space, but some dealers are worried that the acoustics in the warehouse-like new premises will make trading more difficult.

Those worries were voiced on Thursday when the NYMEX, which bills itself as the world's largest energy and metals futures market, arranged a mock trading session in the new 25,000 square-foot space at the World Financial Center, overlooking the Hudson River.
The exchange is due to start trading full-time from the new premises in just three weeks, on May 27.

"The acoustics are not great because the ceilings are so high and the place is not carpeted like the place we have now. Nobody can hear each other," said a crude oil dealer, who was testing out the new floor on Thursday.
The new exchange is divided between two floors, one housing NYMEX energy futures traders, the other the sight of metal trading on NYMEX's Commodity Exchange Inc (COMEX) division.

"We will all be farther away so we will have to shout louder and use hand signals more," said Merrill Lynch trader Howard Hopkins. "Having said that, the kinds of complaints I have been hearing about the exchange can be overcome. It just means that we will have to get used to something new."
NYMEX is moving for the fourth time since it started as the Butter and Cheese Exchange in 1872. Its new location will be a five miute walk from the old trading space in the World Trade Center.

The new space will provide significantly more elbow room for dealers who rely on shouting and aggressive motioning to sell and buy contracts via the "open outcry" system. But, a large cavernous space with no carpeting magnifies the shouting required for trading, dealers complained.
"The place is so much bigger, so it's hard to see the prices on the board," said a gasoline futures trader.
On the upside, dealers said, the booths are nearer to the trading pits, so the phone cords, which currently run to 25 feet and form an annoying web around the pits, are much shorter.
Also, fiber optics are used throughout the communications systems and phones allow more contacts to be programmed into autodial for the instant switching required to do business.
((-- Harry Milling, New York Energy Desk, 212-859-1761))
